title: Extrinsic curvature bias in the small-regularisation limit of Sinkhorn metrics
shortTitle: Sinkhorn metrics on curved data: the extrinsic curvature bias
oneLine: On a curved surface sitting in space, with straight-line transport cost, the Sinkhorn metric converges to the Wasserstein metric as the regularisation ε shrinks, but at small ε it reads short by (ε/4) times a term measuring how the surface bends in space: on a circle of radius R every mode is multiplied by 1 − ε/(4R²), and a cheap positive correction removes the error.
abstract: Entropic (Sinkhorn) optimal transport defines a local Riemannian metric on probability distributions, and as the regularisation ε tends to 0 it should recover Wasserstein geometry. For a smooth positive density on a compact connected submanifold of Euclidean space without boundary, with the fixed ambient cost |x−y|², this candidate proves that the Sinkhorn metric operator converges in operator norm on centred L² to the inverse weighted Laplacian, at rate O(ε^{1/2}) in L² operator norm and O(ε) from H² to L². For a smooth tangent hμ with Aφ = h and A = −ρ⁻¹div(ρ∇), the metric satisfies g_ε(hμ,hμ) = ∫|∇φ|²dμ − (ε/4)∫Σ_α|S_α∇φ|²dμ + O(ε²), where S_α are the shape operators of the embedding. The first bias is therefore nonpositive and depends on the embedding, not only on the intrinsic geometry: the transport cost uses the chord, which is shorter than the arc. On a circle of radius R each eigenvalue is multiplied by 1 − ε/(4R²) to first order, and this order is sharp. A positive correction built from the entropic inverse removes the term; the expansions hold along smooth finite-dimensional density families; round spheres are computed exactly with an explicit ε² coefficient; a high-frequency family on the circle shows that no operator-norm rate better than O(ε) is possible; and isometric embeddings, such as a round circle and an ellipse of equal length, give different biases. The formal limit is due to Lavenant, Luckhardt, Mordant, Schmitzer and Tamanini; operator-level curvature expansions of Gaussian kernels are credited to Smolyanov, von Weizsäcker and Wittich, Liou and Lu, and Guo, whose full text could not be read. Population densities on closed manifolds only. AI-assisted, unrefereed candidate; no external peer review, independent reproduction or formal verification is claimed.

Seven scripts give checks: a symbolic check of the sphere coefficients, 60-digit sphere eigenvalues for S¹ to S⁴, a Funk–Hecke check, the flat torus in R⁴, a torus of revolution at nonconstant density, an equal-length ellipse against the circle, circle operator-norm evidence, a nonuniform ellipse at 768 and 1536 nodes, and independent circle and ellipse implementations. keyResults: Limit and bias (Theorem 2.1): the Sinkhorn metric operator converges in operator norm to the inverse weighted Laplacian, and g_ε(hμ,hμ) = ∫|∇φ|²dμ − (ε/4)∫⟨Q∇φ,∇φ⟩dμ + O(ε²) with Q = Σ_α S_α², the squared shape operators: a nonpositive first bias that depends on the embedding.

Rates (Theorem 2.4): ‖B_ε − A⁻¹‖ = O(ε^{1/2}) in L² operator norm and O(ε) from H² to L²; on the circle no L² operator-norm rate better than O(ε) is possible (Proposition 9.2); whether O(ε) holds in general is open.

Correction and families (Corollary 2.2, Theorem 2.3): a positive corrected metric built from the entropic inverse is accurate to O(ε²) on fixed smooth directions, and all expansions hold along smooth finite-dimensional density families.

Exact cases (Section 9.1, Proposition 9.1): on a circle of radius R each eigenvalue R²/k² becomes (R²/k²)(1 − ε/(4R²)) to first order, so on the unit circle 1/k² becomes (1/k²)(1 − ε/4), and this order is sharp; on round spheres S^m the metric is computed exactly with an explicit ε² coefficient.

Embedding dependence (Proposition 10.1): isometric embeddings give different first-order biases; a round circle and an ellipse of the same length 2π give coefficients −0.125 and −0.043 for φ = cos s, and no closed embedded manifold has Q ≡ 0.

narration: How curved surfaces bias a popular way of measuring distance between distributions. An Evidence Press briefing. Optimal transport compares two probability distributions by the cheapest way of moving one onto the other. Adding a small amount of entropy, a smoothing of strength epsilon, makes this much faster to compute; the result is called Sinkhorn's method. It also gives a local ruler: a way of saying how far apart two nearby distributions are. As epsilon shrinks to zero, that ruler should turn into the classical Wasserstein geometry. This candidate paper proves that it does, for smooth data spread over a closed curved surface sitting in ordinary space, with cost measured along straight lines. It also finds the first error. At small epsilon the ruler reads slightly too short, by epsilon over four times a term that measures how sharply the surface bends in space. The reason is simple: the straight chord between two points is shorter than the arc along the surface. On a circle of radius one, every reading shrinks by the factor one minus epsilon over four. The bias depends on how the surface sits in space, not only on its shape: a round circle and an ellipse of the same length give different biases. A cheap positive correction removes the error. The paper also proves rates of convergence, solves round spheres exactly to second order, and shows that no uniform rate better than epsilon is possible. Related expansions of the underlying operators are credited to earlier work. The results cover continuous densities on closed surfaces with known curvature; there is no sampling theory, and the sharpest rate remains open. This is an unrefereed candidate with internal AI-assisted review only. Released on the fourth of November 2026; the paper, code and data are linked from the release page. This briefing uses an AI-generated voice and is not additional evidence.
